payload.rationale: Resolution requires NASA GISS's unsmoothed annual Land-Ocean Temperature Index for 2026 to exceed both the 2025 value and 1.28°C (the 2024 record value, i.e., effectively a new all-time record at ≥1.29°C in GISS's two-decimal reporting). Background: 2024 set the record (~1.28°C above 1951-1980); 2025 came in slightly below (roughly 1.2x°C) amid ENSO-neutral/weak La Niña conditions. Weak La Niña persisted into early 2026, which typically suppresses global temperatures in the first part of the year; a transition toward neutral or possibly El Niño during 2026 would boost late-year anomalies, but record years usually follow El Niño onset with a lag (e.g., 2023 onset → 2024 record). Institutional outlooks issued around the start of 2026 generally rated a 2026 record as possible but not the most likely outcome, with 2026 more probably landing as the second- or third-warmest year. The underlying warming trend (~0.2°C/decade plus recent excess warmth) keeps a record within reach, and a rapid, strong El Niño in mid-2026 would raise the odds. Too high: if early-2026 La Niña cooling was pronounced and El Niño did not materialize, 2026 is likely locked below 1.28°C by September, making the true probability near 5-10%. Too low: if 2026 months ran as warm as 2024-2025 anomalies suggest (persistent record ocean heat, reduced aerosols) and an El Niño developed by mid-year, the year-to-date could already be tracking at or above record pace, in which case the probability could be 50%+. Without year-to-date GISS data through August 2026, I weight toward the trend/ENSO base rate.
limitations: No supplied evidence or year-to-date 2026 GISS monthly anomalies; ENSO state during 2026 is assumed from general background rather than observed.
Exact GISS 2025 annual value not confirmed; threshold interpretation assumes GISS reports to two decimals so 1.29°C or higher is needed.
Possible GISS methodological or baseline revisions could shift reported values.
